title: Colombia's Catholic Church Strengthens Exorcism Training and Safeguards
site_name: ColombiaOne: News from Colombia and the World
excerpt: Colombia’s Catholic Church is strengthening exorcism training, emphasizing discernment, mental-health support and safeguards.
content:
Colombia’s Catholic Church has tightened its guidelines for exorcisms and strengthened the training of priests who perform them, emphasizing careful discernment, professional support and the protection of human dignity. The approach was highlighted during the third national training course for exorcists, held in Bogota under the motto “Liberar y Cuidar” (Free and Care), which brought together about 80 priests and delegates from ecclesiastical jurisdictions across the country.

Participants studied exorcism, prayers of deliverance, spiritual discernment, pastoral practice and safeguards for vulnerable people. Father Carlos Guillermo Arias Jimenez, who directs the Doctrine Department of Colombia’s Episcopal Conference, explained that the Church does not automatically interpret unusual behavior or experiences as possession or demonic influence.

Instead, priests must follow a process of evaluation and can consult doctors, psychologists or psychiatrists when symptoms may have a medical or mental-health explanation. The Church also treats exorcism as an extraordinary measure rather than a routine response, requiring authorization from a diocesan bishop and a serious assessment before the rite can take place. The approach differs sharply from the dramatic portrayals common in movies and places greater emphasis on discernment, responsibility and care.

What Colombia’s Church requires before an exorcism

The central requirement is discernment, a careful process of evaluating a situation before acting, because the Church demands moral certainty that a possible evil influence exists before a priest performs an exorcism. The process is intended to distinguish cases that a religious perspective might identify as possession from situations with other causes.

Colombia’s Church includes psychology and psychiatry in that process, allowing people who seek help to be referred to specialists when their symptoms point to a psychological or psychiatric condition.

Father Arias also explained that the decisive criterion is the discernment process rather than the dramatic behavior often depicted in films. For that reason, the Church treats exorcism as an extraordinary measure and the final stage of a longer process. Some authorized priests can spend years without performing one.

Not every priest can perform an exorcism. The rite is reserved for a priest authorized by the diocesan bishop, in accordance with the Church’s canon law (its internal legal code). The law calls for the bishop to grant permission only to a priest who is devout, learned, prudent and upright in life.

Candidates must also have a life of prayer, theological training and sound judgment. The ritual itself includes elements such as blessed water.

How exorcism training emphasizes care and protection

Colombia’s Church designed the latest course to strengthen the ministry and distance it from superstition and magic. The program also reflects how the Church’s approach has expanded since earlier editions.

The second course, held in 2022, brought together 110 people from 47 jurisdictions, including bishops, priests, deacons, religious sisters, and lay specialists in psychiatry and psychology. The participation of mental-health professionals reflects the Church’s emphasis on considering medical and psychological factors alongside spiritual discernment.

The 2026 edition continued in that direction, focusing on protocols, abuse prevention and a culture of care for vulnerable people. It also examined ways to avoid hasty spiritual explanations for situations that may involve psychological, medical or social factors.

Father Arias recalled that in 2020 the Vatican’s Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued guidelines for the exorcist’s ministry, and said current training aims to ensure that priests base their actions on serious evaluation rather than suspicion alone.

An exorcist in Colombia can also work with a support team that includes professionals who assist with the discernment process.

Finally, Arias reminded participants that, from the Catholic perspective, evil is not limited to extraordinary cases. It can also appear in everyday realities such as corruption, injustice, lies and harm done to other people.
